rows.stem: The projection vector of vector \(\vec{a}\) on vector \(\vec{b}\) is
rows.solution: The projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is the component of \(\vec{a}\) along the direction of \(\vec{b}\), so it must be a VECTOR pointing along \(\vec{b}\). Its signed length is \(|\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\), and the unit vector along \(\vec{b}\) is \(\dfrac{\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\). Multiplying the two, the projection vector is \(\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\cdot\dfrac{\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = \left(\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\right)\vec{b}\), which is option \(\left(\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\right)\vec{b}\). Note that \(\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\) is only the scalar projection, and the two options carrying \(|\vec{a}|\) in the denominator resolve \(\vec{a}\) along the wrong vector.

rows.stem: The function \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 6\) is increasing in the interval
rows.solution: Differentiate: \(f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 2(x - 2)\). A function is increasing where its derivative is non-negative, so \(f'(x) \ge 0 \iff x \ge 2\). Hence \(f\) is increasing on \([2, \infty)\), which is option \([2, \infty)\). The parabola has its vertex at \(x = 2\) and falls on \((-\infty, 2]\), which is why the option \((-\infty, 2]\) is exactly the interval of DECREASE, and \((0, 2)\) and \([1, 2]\) are sub-intervals of it.

rows.stem: If \(f(2a - x) = f(x)\), then \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx\) is
rows.solution: Split the interval at \(a\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx + \int_a^{2a} f(x)\,dx\). In the second integral substitute \(x = 2a - t\), so \(dx = -dt\) and the limits \(x = a, 2a\) become \(t = a, 0\). This gives \(\displaystyle\int_a^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{a} f(2a - t)\,dt\). Using the given condition \(f(2a - t) = f(t)\), this equals \(\displaystyle\int_0^{a} f(t)\,dt\). Hence the whole integral is \(2\displaystyle\int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx\), which is option \(2\displaystyle\int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx\).

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 12 & 4y \\ 6x & 5 & 2x \\ 8x & 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) is a symmetric matrix, then \((2x + y)\) is
rows.solution: A matrix is symmetric when \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\) for every pair of entries. Comparing the three off-diagonal pairs: from \(a_{12} = a_{21}\), \(12 = 6x\), so \(x = 2\); from \(a_{23} = a_{32}\), \(2x = 4\), which gives the same \(x = 2\) and so is consistent; from \(a_{13} = a_{31}\), \(4y = 8x = 16\), so \(y = 4\). Therefore \(2x + y = 4 + 4 = 8\), which is option \(8\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: If \(y = \sin^{-1} x\), \(-1 \le x \le 0\), then the range of y is
rows.solution: The principal-value branch of \(\sin^{-1}\) is \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), and on it \(\sin^{-1}\) is increasing. So the range over \(-1 \le x \le 0\) runs from \(\sin^{-1}(-1)\) up to \(\sin^{-1}(0)\), that is from \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(0\). Both endpoints of the domain are INCLUDED, and both values are attained, so the range is the CLOSED interval \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right]\), which is option \(\left[\dfrac{-\pi}{2}, 0\right]\). The three options that open a bracket at one end or the other wrongly exclude an attained value.

rows.stem: If a line makes angles of \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\theta\) with the positive directions of \(x\), y and z-axis respectively, then \(\theta\) is
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: the official answer for this question reads in full "No option is correct. Full marks may be awarded for attempting the question." None of the four printed alternatives is the answer, so no key is given; the correct value is derived below.] If a line makes angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) with the positive directions of the axes, its direction cosines satisfy \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\). Here \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \cos^2\theta = 1\), giving \(\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(\cos\theta = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}\). An angle a line makes with an axis lies in \([0, \pi]\), and BOTH signs are admissible there: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). So the complete answer is \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) or \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), and this is why no option fits: \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) only is incomplete because it discards the second branch; \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) is wrong because \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) lies outside \([0, \pi]\) and so is not an angle with an axis, while the genuine second branch \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) is missing; \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) only fails for the same reason; and \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) fails since \(\cos^2\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{3}{4} \ne \dfrac{1}{4}\).

rows.stem: If E and F are two events such that \(P(E) > 0\) and \(P(F) \ne 1\), then \(P(\overline{E}/\overline{F})\) is
rows.solution: By the definition of conditional probability, \(P(\overline{E}/\overline{F}) = \dfrac{P(\overline{E} \cap \overline{F})}{P(\overline{F})}\), which is legitimate because \(P(F) \ne 1\) makes \(P(\overline{F}) \ne 0\). By De Morgan's law \(\overline{E} \cap \overline{F} = \overline{E \cup F}\), so the numerator is \(P(\overline{E \cup F}) = 1 - P(E \cup F)\). Hence \(P(\overline{E}/\overline{F}) = \dfrac{1 - P(E \cup F)}{P(\overline{F})}\), which is option \(\dfrac{1 - P(E \cup F)}{P(\overline{F})}\). The option \(1 - P(E/F)\) equals \(P(\overline{E}/F)\), which conditions on \(F\) rather than on \(\overline{F}\); the option \(1 - P(\overline{E}/F)\) equals \(P(E/F)\) for the same reason; and \(\dfrac{P(\overline{E})}{P(\overline{F})}\) would need \(E\) and \(F\) to be independent, which is not given.

rows.stem: Which of the following can be both a symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix ?
rows.solution: Suppose a matrix \(A\) is both symmetric and skew-symmetric. Symmetry gives \(A^T = A\) and skew-symmetry gives \(A^T = -A\). Equating the two, \(A = -A\), so \(2A = O\) and hence \(A = O\). The only such matrix is therefore the Null Matrix, which is option Null Matrix. A Unit Matrix and a general Diagonal Matrix are symmetric but not skew-symmetric (their non-zero diagonal entries would have to satisfy \(a_{ii} = -a_{ii}\)), and a Row Matrix is not even square, so neither condition can apply to it.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: The equation of a line parallel to the vector \(3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) and passing through the point \((4, -3, 7)\) is :
rows.solution: A line through the point \((x_0, y_0, z_0)\) parallel to \(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}\) has parametric equations \(x = at + x_0\), \(y = bt + y_0\), \(z = ct + z_0\). Here the direction ratios are \(3, 1, 2\) and the point is \((4, -3, 7)\), so \(x = 3t + 4\), \(y = t - 3\), \(z = 2t + 7\), which is option \(x = 3t + 4, y = t - 3, z = 2t + 7\). Two checks separate it from the near-misses: putting \(t = 0\) must return the given point, which rules out the options carrying \(y = t + 3\) and \(y = -t + 3\) since both give \(y = 3\) instead of \(-3\); and the coefficients of \(t\) must be \(3, 1, 2\) in that order, which rules out \(x = 4t + 3, y = -3t + 1, z = 7t + 2\), where the point and the direction ratios have been interchanged.

rows.stem:
Four friends Abhay, Bina, Chhaya and Devesh were asked to simplify \(4\,AB + 3(AB + BA) - 4\,BA\), where A and B are both matrices of order \(2 \times 2\). It is known that \(A \ne B \ne I\) and \(A^{-1} \ne B\).
Their answers are given as :
Abhay : \(6\,AB\)
Bina : \(7\,AB - BA\)
Chhaya : \(8\,AB\)
Devesh : \(7\,BA - AB\)
Who answered it correctly ?
rows.solution:
Matrix addition is associative and commutative and scalar multiplication distributes over it, so the expression can be expanded term by term: \(4\,AB + 3(AB + BA) - 4\,BA = 4\,AB + 3\,AB + 3\,BA - 4\,BA = 7\,AB - BA\). This is Bina's answer, so the correct option is Bina. The point of the conditions \(A 
e B 
e I\) and \(A^{-1} 
e B\) is that matrix multiplication is NOT commutative in general, so \(AB\) and \(BA\) may not be combined: doing so would collapse \(7\,AB - BA\) to \(6\,AB\), which is Abhay's answer, while adding the two terms instead gives Chhaya's \(8\,AB\). Devesh's \(7\,BA - AB\) has the two products interchanged.

rows.stem: A cylindrical tank of radius 10 cm is being filled with sugar at the rate of \(100\,\pi\) cm\(^3\)/s. The rate, at which the height of the sugar inside the tank is increasing, is :
rows.solution: The sugar fills a cylinder of fixed radius \(r = 10\) cm, so its volume at height \(h\) is \(V = \pi r^2 h = 100\pi h\). The radius is constant, so differentiating with respect to time gives \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 100\pi\,\dfrac{dh}{dt}\). We are given \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 100\pi\) cm\(^3\)/s, so \(100\pi = 100\pi\,\dfrac{dh}{dt}\), giving \(\dfrac{dh}{dt} = 1\). The height rises at 1 cm/s, which is option 1 cm/s.

rows.stem: Let \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\) be two unit vectors and \(\alpha\) be the angle between them. Then \((\vec{p} + \vec{q})\) will be a unit vector for what value of \(\alpha\) ?
rows.solution: Since \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\) are unit vectors, \(|\vec{p}| = |\vec{q}| = 1\) and \(\vec{p} \cdot \vec{q} = \cos\alpha\). Expanding the square of the magnitude of the sum, \(|\vec{p} + \vec{q}|^2 = |\vec{p}|^2 + |\vec{q}|^2 + 2\,\vec{p} \cdot \vec{q} = 1 + 1 + 2\cos\alpha\). Requiring \(\vec{p} + \vec{q}\) to be a unit vector means \(|\vec{p} + \vec{q}|^2 = 1\), so \(2 + 2\cos\alpha = 1\), giving \(\cos\alpha = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and hence \(\alpha = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), which is option \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). The angle between two vectors is taken in \([0, \pi]\), so this is the only solution; note the answer is obtuse, since two unit vectors must lean away from each other for their sum to shrink back to length 1.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: The line \(x = 1 + 5\mu\), \(y = -5 + \mu\), \(z = -6 - 3\mu\) passes through which of the following point ?
rows.solution: A point lies on the line exactly when a SINGLE value of \(\mu\) reproduces all three coordinates. Taking \(\mu = 0\) gives \(x = 1\), \(y = -5\), \(z = -6\), so the line passes through \((1, -5, -6)\), which is option \((1, -5, -6)\). The other three fail on the \(z\)-coordinate or worse: \(z = -6 - 3\mu = 6\) forces \(\mu = -4\), and that value gives \(x = 1 + 5(-4) = -19\) and \(y = -5 - 4 = -9\), matching none of \((1, -5, 6)\), \((1, 5, 6)\) or \((-1, -5, 6)\).

rows.stem: If A denotes the set of continuous functions and B denotes set of differentiable functions, then which of the following depicts the correct relation between set A and B ?

options.label: A
options.text: A Venn diagram in which circle A lies entirely inside circle B

options.label: B
options.text: A Venn diagram in which circle B lies entirely inside circle A

options.label: C
options.text: A Venn diagram in which circles A and B overlap partially

options.label: D
options.text: A Venn diagram in which circles A and B are disjoint

rows.figure: REQUIRED — all four options are printed as Venn DIAGRAMS with no accompanying words. Page idx 10; the same four diagrams are reprinted in the marking scheme at ms/p05, where the key is the diagram with B inside A.
rows.solution: The four alternatives are printed as Venn diagrams, so the question is asking which containment holds between the set \(A\) of continuous functions and the set \(B\) of differentiable functions. If a function is differentiable at a point then it is continuous there, so every differentiable function is continuous and \(B \subseteq A\). The converse is false: \(f(x) = |x|\) is continuous everywhere but has no derivative at \(x = 0\), so \(A\) contains members that \(B\) does not and the containment is strict. Hence the correct picture is the one in which circle B lies entirely inside circle A, which is option "A Venn diagram in which circle B lies entirely inside circle A". The reverse containment would claim every continuous function is differentiable, the partially overlapping diagram would claim some differentiable function is discontinuous, and the disjoint diagram would claim no differentiable function is continuous.

rows.stem: The area of the shaded region (figure) represented by the curves \(y = x^2\), \(0 \le x \le 2\) and y-axis is given by
rows.figure: REQUIRED — the stem says "the shaded region (figure)" and the printed graph is what fixes WHICH region is meant: the hatching runs between the y-axis and the curve with y from 0 to 4, not the region under the curve. Page idx 10 (reprinted at ms/p05).
rows.solution: In the printed figure the hatching lies between the \(y\)-axis and the curve \(y = x^2\), i.e. to the LEFT of the curve, running from \(y = 0\) up to \(y = 4\) (the height of the curve at \(x = 2\)). For such a region it is the horizontal strips that are simple: at height \(y\) the strip runs from \(x = 0\) to the curve, where \(x = \sqrt{y}\), so its width is \(\sqrt{y}\). Integrating these widths as \(y\) goes from \(0\) to \(4\) gives the area as \(\displaystyle\int_0^{4} \sqrt{y}\,dy\), which is option \(\displaystyle\int_0^{4} \sqrt{y}\,dy\). Two checks confirm the reading: the limits must be the \(y\)-values \(0\) to \(4\), not the \(x\)-values \(0\) to \(2\), and \(\displaystyle\int_0^{4} \sqrt{y}\,dy = \dfrac{16}{3}\) while the option \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2} x^2\,dx = \dfrac{8}{3}\) is the complementary region UNDER the curve; the two add to \(8\), the area of the enclosing \(2 \times 4\) rectangle.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem: A factory produces two products X and Y. The profit earned by selling X and Y is represented by the objective function \(Z = 5x + 7y\), where \(x\) and y are the number of units of X and Y respectively sold. Which of the following statement is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: The objective function maximizes the difference of the profit earned from products X and Y.

options.label: B
options.text: The objective function measures the total production of products X and Y.

options.label: C
options.text: The objective function maximizes the combined profit earned from selling X and Y.

options.label: D
options.text: The objective function ensures the company produces more of product X than product Y.

rows.solution: In a linear programming problem the objective function is the quantity being optimised, and here each unit of X contributes 5 and each unit of Y contributes 7 to profit. So \(Z = 5x + 7y\) is the TOTAL profit from selling \(x\) units of X and \(y\) units of Y, and maximising \(Z\) maximises that combined profit. The correct statement is therefore "The objective function maximizes the combined profit earned from selling X and Y." The other three misread the function: a difference of profits would need a minus sign between the terms; total PRODUCTION would be \(x + y\), with the coefficients dropped, since 5 and 7 are rupees per unit and not counts; and nothing in \(Z\) forces \(x > y\), because which product it pays to make more of is settled by the constraints, not by the objective function.

rows.stem: If A and B are square matrices of order m such that \(A^2 - B^2 = (A - B)(A + B)\), then which of the following is always correct ?
rows.solution: Expand the right-hand side using distributivity, being careful NOT to commute the products: \((A - B)(A + B) = A^2 + AB - BA - B^2\). Setting this equal to the given \(A^2 - B^2\) and cancelling \(A^2\) and \(-B^2\) leaves \(AB - BA = O\), that is \(AB = BA\), which is option \(AB = BA\). So the identity \(A^2 - B^2 = (A - B)(A + B)\), familiar from numbers, holds for matrices exactly when the two commute. The other options are sufficient but not necessary: \(A = B\), \(A = O\) or \(B = O\), and \(A = I\) or \(B = I\) each force commuting, so each makes the identity true, but none of them is forced BY it — any two distinct commuting matrices, such as \(A\) and \(A^2\), satisfy the identity while satisfying none of those three.

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem: If p and q are respectively the order and degree of the differential equation \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 0\), then \((p - q)\) is
rows.solution: First carry out the outer differentiation, because order and degree are read off the equation only once it is written as a polynomial in the derivatives. By the chain rule, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 3\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the equation is \(3\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0\). The highest derivative appearing is \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is \(p = 2\); the equation is already polynomial in the derivatives and the power of that highest derivative is 1, so the degree is \(q = 1\). Note the degree is decided by the exponent of the HIGHEST derivative alone, not by the \(\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\) factor. Hence \(p - q = 2 - 1 = 1\), which is option \(1\).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(A = \text{diag}\,[\,3\ \ 5\ \ 2\,]\) is a scalar matrix of order \(3 \times 3\).
Reason (R) : If a diagonal matrix has all non-zero elements equal, it is known as a scalar matrix.
rows.context:
ASSERTION – REASON BASED QUESTIONS
Direction : Question number 19 and 20 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and the Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Test the two statements separately. A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are ALL EQUAL. Here \(A = \text{diag}\,[\,3\ \ 5\ \ 2\,]\) has diagonal entries \(3, 5, 2\), which are unequal, so \(A\) is a diagonal matrix of order \(3 \times 3\) but not a scalar one: the Assertion is FALSE. The Reason states the definition of a scalar matrix correctly, so it is TRUE. With a false Assertion and a true Reason, the correct choice is "Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true." Note that the Reason is exactly the test the Assertion fails, which is what makes the pairing instructive rather than accidental.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Every point of the feasible region of a Linear Programming Problem is an optimal solution.
Reason (R) : The optimal solution for a Linear Programming Problem exists only at one or more corner point(s) of the feasible region.
rows.context:
ASSERTION – REASON BASED QUESTIONS
Direction : Question number 19 and 20 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and the Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Test the two statements separately. The Assertion claims every point of the feasible region is optimal, which is false: for the feasible region of a typical problem the objective function takes different values at different feasible points, so only some of them optimise it. (An objective function constant over the whole region is the degenerate exception, not the rule.) The Reason states the corner-point theorem: when an optimal value exists it is attained at a corner point, and if it is attained at two corners then at every point of the joining edge as well. That is true. With a false Assertion and a true Reason, the correct choice is "Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true." The Reason is in fact what refutes the Assertion, since it confines the optimum to the boundary corners rather than spreading it over the region.

rows.stem: A vector \(\vec{a}\) makes equal angles with all the three axes. If the magnitude of the vector is \(5\sqrt{3}\) units, then find \(\vec{a}\).
rows.solution: Let \(\alpha\) be the common angle that \(\vec{a}\) makes with each of the three axes. Its direction cosines are then all equal, \(l = m = n = \cos\alpha\), and they must satisfy \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\), so \(3\cos^2\alpha = 1\) and \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Hence the unit vector along \(\vec{a}\) is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\). A vector is its magnitude times its unit vector, so \(\vec{a} = 5\sqrt{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 5(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\). As a check, \(|5(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})| = 5\sqrt{3}\) and each component is equal, so the angles with the three axes agree. [Note: \(3\cos^2\alpha = 1\) also allows \(\cos\alpha = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), giving \(\vec{a} = -5(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\); this vector likewise has magnitude \(5\sqrt{3}\) and makes equal (obtuse) angles with all three axes, so it is a second valid answer. The marking scheme records only the positive branch, and \(5(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) is the expected answer.]

rows.stem: If \(\vec{\alpha}\) and \(\vec{\beta}\) are position vectors of two points P and Q respectively, then find the position vector of a point R in QP produced such that \(QR = \dfrac{3}{2} QP\).
rows.solution: "R in QP produced" means R lies on the ray from Q through P, BEYOND P, so \(\overrightarrow{QR}\) points the same way as \(\overrightarrow{QP}\) and the given length relation becomes the vector equation \(\overrightarrow{QR} = \dfrac{3}{2}\overrightarrow{QP}\). Now \(\overrightarrow{QP} = \vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta}\), so taking \(\vec{x}\) as the position vector of R, \(\vec{x} - \vec{\beta} = \dfrac{3}{2}(\vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta})\), which gives \(\vec{x} = \vec{\beta} + \dfrac{3}{2}\vec{\alpha} - \dfrac{3}{2}\vec{\beta} = \dfrac{3\vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta}}{2}\). Equivalently, in the language of the section formula, R divides PQ EXTERNALLY in the ratio \(1 : 3\), and the external-division formula gives the same position vector \(\dfrac{1 \cdot \vec{\beta} - 3 \cdot \vec{\alpha}}{1 - 3} = \dfrac{3\vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta}}{2}\). As a check, \(\overrightarrow{QR} = \dfrac{3\vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta}}{2} - \vec{\beta} = \dfrac{3}{2}(\vec{\alpha} - \vec{\beta})\), as required, and R lies past P since \(\dfrac{3}{2} > 1\).

rows.stem: Evaluate : \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} \sqrt{1 + \sin 2x}\;dx\)
rows.solution: The point of the question is to recognise the expression under the root as a perfect square. Since \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\) and \(2\sin x\cos x = \sin 2x\), we have \(1 + \sin 2x = (\sin x + \cos x)^2\). Hence the integral is \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} \sqrt{(\sin x + \cos x)^2}\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/4} |\sin x + \cos x|\,dx\), and on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\) both \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are non-negative, so the modulus may simply be dropped. Integrating, \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} (\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = \Big[-\cos x + \sin x\Big]_0^{\pi/4}\). At the upper limit this is \(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\) and at the lower limit it is \(-1 + 0 = -1\), so the value of the integral is \(0 - (-1) = 1\).

rows.stem: Find the values of ‘a’ for which \(f(x) = \sin x - ax + b\) is increasing on R.
rows.solution: Differentiate: \(f'(x) = \cos x - a\) (the constant \(b\) plays no part). For \(f\) to be increasing on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) we need \(f'(x) \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), i.e. \(\cos x \ge a\) for every \(x\). This must hold even where \(\cos x\) is SMALLEST, so \(a\) must not exceed the minimum value of \(\cos x\). Since \(-1 \le \cos x \le 1\), that minimum is \(-1\), and the condition becomes \(a \le -1\). Hence \(a \in (-\infty, -1]\). The endpoint is genuinely admissible: at \(a = -1\), \(f'(x) = \cos x + 1 \ge 0\), vanishing only at the isolated points \(x = (2k+1)\pi\), and a derivative that is zero only at isolated points still leaves the function increasing. [Note: the marking scheme records \(a \in (-\infty, -1]\) and adds that \(a \in (-\infty, -1)\) may also be accepted, for candidates applying the stricter requirement \(f'(x) > 0\) everywhere.]

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are two non-collinear vectors, then find \(x\), such that \(\vec{\alpha} = (x - 2)\,\vec{a} + \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{\beta} = (3 + 2x)\,\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\) are collinear.
rows.solution: Two vectors expressed in the same non-collinear pair \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) are collinear exactly when their components are proportional, so \(\vec{\alpha}\) and \(\vec{\beta}\) are collinear when \(\dfrac{x - 2}{3 + 2x} = \dfrac{1}{-2}\). (Equivalently, \(\vec{\beta} = \lambda\vec{\alpha}\) forces \(3 + 2x = \lambda(x - 2)\) and \(-2 = \lambda\), and eliminating \(\lambda\) gives the same equation; the hypothesis that \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are non-collinear is what lets us compare components at all, since it makes the representation unique.) Cross-multiplying, \(-2(x - 2) = 3 + 2x\), so \(-2x + 4 = 3 + 2x\), giving \(1 = 4x\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{4}\). Checking, \(x = \dfrac{1}{4}\) makes \(\vec{\alpha} = -\dfrac{7}{4}\vec{a} + \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{\beta} = \dfrac{7}{2}\vec{a} - 2\vec{b} = -2\vec{\alpha}\), which are indeed collinear.

rows.stem: If \(x = e^{\frac{x}{y}}\), then prove that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x \log x}\).
rows.solution: The exponent is awkward to differentiate directly, so take logarithms first to bring \(y\) down. From \(x = e^{x/y}\), taking natural logs gives \(\log x = \dfrac{x}{y}\), and clearing the denominator gives the convenient implicit form \(y \log x = x\). Now differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on the left: \(y \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} + \log x \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\), i.e. \(\dfrac{y}{x} + \log x\,\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\). Rearranging, \(\log x\,\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 - \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{x - y}{x}\), and dividing by \(\log x\) gives \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x \log x}\), as required.

rows.stem:
If \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x - 3, & -3 \le x \le -2 \\ x + 1, & -2 < x \le 0 \end{cases}\)
Check the differentiability of \(f(x)\) at \(x = -2\).
rows.solution: The point \(x = -2\) is where the definition changes, so compare the one-sided derivatives there. The value at the point comes from the first branch, since \(-2\) is included in \(-3 \le x \le -2\): \(f(-2) = 2(-2) - 3 = -7\). For the LEFT-hand derivative, take \(h > 0\) so that \(-2 - h\) is in the first branch: \(Lf'(-2) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(-2 - h) - f(-2)}{-h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{[2(-2 - h) - 3] - (-7)}{-h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{-2h}{-h} = 2\). For the RIGHT-hand derivative, \(-2 + h\) is in the second branch: \(Rf'(-2) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(-2 + h) - f(-2)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{[(-2 + h) + 1] - (-7)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{6 + h}{h}\), which does not exist because the numerator tends to \(6\) while the denominator tends to \(0\). Since the right-hand derivative does not exist, \(f\) is NOT differentiable at \(x = -2\). The underlying reason is a jump: \(f(-2) = -7\) while \(f(x) \to -1\) as \(x \to -2^{+}\), so \(f\) is not even continuous at \(-2\), and a function that is discontinuous at a point cannot be differentiable there.

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation \(2(y + 3) - xy \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\); given \(y(1) = -2\).
rows.solution: The equation separates. Writing it as \(xy\,\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2(y + 3)\) and dividing, \(\dfrac{y}{y + 3}\,dy = \dfrac{2}{x}\,dx\). The left side is an improper fraction, so split it first: \(\dfrac{y}{y + 3} = 1 - \dfrac{3}{y + 3}\). Integrating both sides, \(\displaystyle\int\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{y + 3}\right)dy = 2\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\), which gives \(y - 3\log|y + 3| = 2\log|x| + C\). Now apply the initial condition \(y = -2\) when \(x = 1\): the left side is \(-2 - 3\log|1| = -2\) and the right side is \(2\log|1| + C = C\), so \(C = -2\). Hence the required particular solution is \(y - 3\log|y + 3| = 2\log|x| - 2\).

rows.stem:
Solve the following differential equation :
\((1 + x^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2xy = 4x^2\).
rows.solution: Divide through by \(1 + x^2\) to reach the standard linear form \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\,y = \dfrac{4x^2}{1 + x^2}\), which is linear in \(y\) with \(P = \dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\). The integrating factor is \(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}dx} = e^{\log(1 + x^2)} = 1 + x^2\). Multiplying by it returns the left side to the exact derivative \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[y(1 + x^2)\big]\), and the right side simplifies because the \(1 + x^2\) cancels. So \(y(1 + x^2) = \displaystyle\int 4x^2\,dx = \dfrac{4}{3}x^3 + C\). Hence the general solution is \(y(1 + x^2) = \dfrac{4x^3}{3} + C\), or explicitly \(y = \dfrac{4x^3}{3(1 + x^2)} + \dfrac{C}{1 + x^2}\). (Notice that recognising \(2x\) as the derivative of \(1 + x^2\) is what makes the integrating factor come out in closed form.)

rows.stem: Let R be a relation defined over N, where N is set of natural numbers, defined as “mRn if and only if m is a multiple of n, m, n \(\in\) N.” Find whether R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive or not.
rows.solution:
Here \(mRn\) means \(m\) is a multiple of \(n\), i.e. \(m = kn\) for some \(k \in \mathbb{N}\). Test each property in turn.
REFLEXIVE: for any \(x \in \mathbb{N}\), \(x = 1 \cdot x\), so \(x\) is a multiple of itself and \(xRx\) holds for every \(x\). Hence R IS reflexive.
SYMMETRIC: one counter-example is enough. Take \(m = 8\) and \(n = 2\). Then \(8 = 4 \cdot 2\), so \(8R2\); but \(2\) is not a multiple of \(8\), so \(2\) is not R-related to \(8\). Hence R is NOT symmetric.
TRANSITIVE: suppose \(xRy\) and \(yRz\), so \(x = my\) and \(y = nz\) for some \(m, n \in \mathbb{N}\). Substituting, \(x = m(nz) = (mn)z\), and \(p = mn \in \mathbb{N}\), so \(x\) is a multiple of \(z\) and \(xRz\). Hence R IS transitive.
So R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; being reflexive and transitive without symmetry, it is a partial order rather than an equivalence relation.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :
Minimise \(Z = x - 5y\)
subject to the constraints :
\(x - y \ge 0\)
\(-x + 2y \ge 2\)
\(x \ge 3,\ y \le 4,\ y \ge 0\)
rows.solution:
Draw the boundary lines \(x - y = 0\), \(-x + 2y = 2\), \(x = 3\) and \(y = 4\), and shade the side of each that satisfies its inequality. The feasible region is the quadrilateral bounded on the left by \(x = 3\), below by \(x - y = 0\) (since \(x - y \ge 0\) means \(y \le x\)), above by \(y = 4\), and on the right by \(-x + 2y = 2\) (since \(-x + 2y \ge 2\) means \(y \ge \dfrac{x + 2}{2}\)); it is bounded, so a minimum exists and by the corner-point method it is attained at a vertex.
Finding the vertices: \(x = 3\) meets \(-x + 2y = 2\) at \(2y = 5\), giving \(A(3, 2.5)\); \(x = 3\) meets \(x - y = 0\) at \(B(3, 3)\); \(x - y = 0\) meets \(y = 4\) at \(C(4, 4)\); and \(-x + 2y = 2\) meets \(y = 4\) at \(-x + 8 = 2\), giving \(D(6, 4)\).
Evaluating \(Z = x - 5y\) at each corner: at \(A(3, 2.5)\), \(Z = 3 - 12.5 = -9.5\); at \(B(3, 3)\), \(Z = 3 - 15 = -12\); at \(C(4, 4)\), \(Z = 4 - 20 = -16\); at \(D(6, 4)\), \(Z = 6 - 20 = -14\).
The smallest of these is \(-16\), so the minimum value of \(Z\) is \(-16\), attained at \(x = 4\), \(y = 4\).

rows.stem: If \(y = \log\left(\sqrt{x} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^2\), then show that \(x(x + 1)^2\,y_2 + (x + 1)^2\,y_1 = 2\).
rows.solution: Simplify the logarithm before differentiating. Since \(\sqrt{x} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x}}\), we get \(y = \log\left(\dfrac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^2 = 2\log(x + 1) - 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\log x = 2\log(x + 1) - \log x\). Differentiating, \(y_1 = \dfrac{2}{x + 1} - \dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{2x - (x + 1)}{x(x + 1)} = \dfrac{x - 1}{x(x + 1)}\). Multiplying by \((x + 1)\) gives the convenient relation \((x + 1)y_1 = \dfrac{x - 1}{x} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x}\). Differentiate this relation, using the product rule on the left: \((x + 1)y_2 + y_1 = \dfrac{1}{x^2}\). Now multiply throughout by \(x(x + 1)\): \(x(x + 1)^2 y_2 + x(x + 1)y_1 = \dfrac{x(x + 1)}{x^2} = \dfrac{x + 1}{x} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{x}\). The relation above gives \(\dfrac{1}{x} = 1 - (x + 1)y_1\), so the right-hand side is \(1 + 1 - (x + 1)y_1 = 2 - (x + 1)y_1\). Taking that term across, \(x(x + 1)^2 y_2 + x(x + 1)y_1 + (x + 1)y_1 = 2\), and the two middle terms combine as \((x + 1)y_1(x + 1) = (x + 1)^2 y_1\). Hence \(x(x + 1)^2 y_2 + (x + 1)^2 y_1 = 2\), as required.

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: If \(x\sqrt{1 + y} + y\sqrt{1 + x} = 0\), \(-1 < x < 1\), \(x \ne y\), then prove that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-1}{(1 + x)^2}\).
rows.solution: Rather than differentiate implicitly through two square roots, first solve the relation for \(y\). From \(x\sqrt{1 + y} + y\sqrt{1 + x} = 0\) we get \(x\sqrt{1 + y} = -y\sqrt{1 + x}\), and squaring both sides gives \(x^2(1 + y) = y^2(1 + x)\). Rearranging, \(x^2 - y^2 + x^2 y - x y^2 = 0\), which factors as \((x - y)(x + y) + xy(x - y) = 0\), i.e. \((x - y)(x + y + xy) = 0\). We are given \(x \ne y\), so the first factor cannot vanish and therefore \(x + y + xy = 0\). Solving for \(y\), \(y(1 + x) = -x\), so \(y = \dfrac{-x}{1 + x}\) (legitimate since \(-1 < x < 1\) makes \(1 + x \ne 0\)). Differentiating by the quotient rule, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{(1 + x)(1) - x(1)}{(1 + x)^2} = \dfrac{-1}{(1 + x)^2}\), as required. (Squaring can introduce extraneous roots, so it is worth checking that this branch really satisfies the original equation: with \(y = \dfrac{-x}{1 + x}\), \(x\) and \(y\) have opposite signs throughout \(-1 < x < 1\), which is exactly what \(x\sqrt{1 + y} = -y\sqrt{1 + x}\) requires, and substituting, for instance, \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}, y = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) satisfies the given equation.)

rows.stem: A die with number 1 to 6 is biased such that \(P(2) = \dfrac{3}{10}\) and probability of other numbers is equal. Find the mean of the number of times number 2 appears on the dice, if the dice is thrown twice.
rows.solution:
On a single throw \(P(2) = \dfrac{3}{10}\), so the probability of NOT getting a 2 is \(1 - \dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10}\). (The five other faces share this equally, at \(\dfrac{7}{50}\) each, but only the combined figure is needed.) Let \(X\) be the number of times 2 appears in two throws, so \(X = 0, 1, 2\), and the throws are independent.
\(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{7}{10} \times \dfrac{7}{10} = \dfrac{49}{100}\).
\(P(X = 1) = 2 \times \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{7}{10} = \dfrac{42}{100}\), the factor 2 covering the two orders in which the single 2 can occur.
\(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{9}{100}\).
These sum to \(\dfrac{49 + 42 + 9}{100} = 1\), as they must. The mean is \(\sum x\,P(X = x) = 0 \times \dfrac{49}{100} + 1 \times \dfrac{42}{100} + 2 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = \dfrac{42 + 18}{100} = \dfrac{60}{100} = 0.6\). This agrees with the binomial mean \(np = 2 \times \dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

rows.stem:
Two dice are thrown. Defined are the following two events A and B :
\(A = \{(x, y) : x + y = 9\}\), \(B = \{(x, y) : x \ne 3\}\), where \((x, y)\) denote a point in the sample space.
Check if events A and B are independent or mutually exclusive.
rows.solution:
Two dice give a sample space of \(36\) equally likely ordered pairs.
Event A is \(x + y = 9\), so \(A = \{(3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3)\}\) and \(P(A) = \dfrac{4}{36} = \dfrac{1}{9}\).
Event B is \(x \ne 3\); the first die can be any of the five values other than 3 and the second any of 6, so B has \(5 \times 6 = 30\) outcomes and \(P(B) = \dfrac{30}{36} = \dfrac{5}{6}\).
For the intersection, drop from A the one outcome with \(x = 3\): \(A \cap B = \{(4,5), (5,4), (6,3)\}\), so \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{1}{12}\).
INDEPENDENCE requires \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)\). Here \(P(A) \times P(B) = \dfrac{1}{9} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{5}{54}\), whereas \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{4.5}{54}\). Since \(\dfrac{5}{54} \ne \dfrac{1}{12}\), A and B are NOT independent.
MUTUAL EXCLUSIVITY requires \(A \cap B = \varnothing\). Here \(A \cap B\) contains three outcomes, so it is non-empty and A and B are NOT mutually exclusive.
Hence the two events are neither independent nor mutually exclusive.

rows.stem: Find : \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x} \sqrt{\dfrac{x + a}{x - a}}\;dx\).
rows.solution: The standard move is to rationalise the surd so that the denominator becomes \(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\). Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by \(x + a\): \(\sqrt{\dfrac{x + a}{x - a}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(x + a)^2}{(x - a)(x + a)}} = \dfrac{x + a}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}}\), valid on the domain \(x > a > 0\) where both \(x + a\) and \(x^2 - a^2\) are positive. So \(I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x} \cdot \dfrac{x + a}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}}\,dx\), and splitting the numerator over \(x\) turns this into two standard integrals: \(I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}}\,dx + a\int \dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}}\,dx\). The first is \(\log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\right|\) and the second is \(\dfrac{1}{a}\sec^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)\), whose \(\dfrac{1}{a}\) cancels the \(a\) in front. Hence \(I = \log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\right| + \sec^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right) + C\).

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Using integration, find the area of the region bounded by the line \(y = 5x + 2\), the \(x\) – axis and the ordinates \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\).
rows.solution:
Sketch the line \(y = 5x + 2\) between \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\). It crosses the \(x\)-axis where \(5x + 2 = 0\), i.e. at \(x = -\dfrac{2}{5}\), so the region falls into two triangles: on \(\left[-2, -\dfrac{2}{5}\right]\) the line lies BELOW the axis and on \(\left[-\dfrac{2}{5}, 2\right]\) it lies above. Area is a positive quantity, so the two parts must be added in magnitude and not allowed to cancel:
\(\text{Area} = \left|\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{-2/5} (5x + 2)\,dx\right| + \displaystyle\int_{-2/5}^{2} (5x + 2)\,dx\).
An antiderivative of \(5x + 2\) is \(\dfrac{(5x + 2)^2}{10}\), which is convenient because it vanishes exactly at \(x = -\dfrac{2}{5}\).
For the first piece, \(\left[\dfrac{(5x + 2)^2}{10}\right]_{-2}^{-2/5} = 0 - \dfrac{(-8)^2}{10} = -\dfrac{64}{10}\), whose magnitude is \(\dfrac{64}{10}\).
For the second piece, \(\left[\dfrac{(5x + 2)^2}{10}\right]_{-2/5}^{2} = \dfrac{12^2}{10} - 0 = \dfrac{144}{10}\).
Hence the required area is \(\dfrac{64}{10} + \dfrac{144}{10} = \dfrac{208}{10} = \dfrac{104}{5}\) square units. As a check, the two triangles have areas \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{8}{5} \times 8 = \dfrac{32}{5}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{12}{5} \times 12 = \dfrac{72}{5}\), which also total \(\dfrac{104}{5}\).

rows.stem: Find : \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2 + x + 1}{(x + 2)(x^2 + 1)}\;dx\).
rows.solution: The denominator has a linear factor and an irreducible quadratic factor, so the partial-fraction form must carry a LINEAR numerator over the quadratic: \(\dfrac{x^2 + x + 1}{(x + 2)(x^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{A}{x + 2} + \dfrac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 1}\). Clearing denominators, \(x^2 + x + 1 = A(x^2 + 1) + (Bx + C)(x + 2)\). Putting \(x = -2\) kills the second term and gives \(4 - 2 + 1 = 5A\), so \(A = \dfrac{3}{5}\). Comparing coefficients of \(x^2\) gives \(1 = A + B\), so \(B = \dfrac{2}{5}\); comparing constant terms gives \(1 = A + 2C\), so \(2C = \dfrac{2}{5}\) and \(C = \dfrac{1}{5}\). Hence the integral splits as \(\dfrac{3}{5}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x + 2}\,dx + \dfrac{1}{5}\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx + \dfrac{1}{5}\int \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1}\,dx\), where the middle term is written with \(2x\) on top because that is exactly the derivative of \(x^2 + 1\). Integrating each, the answer is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\log|x + 2| + \dfrac{1}{5}\log(x^2 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{5}\tan^{-1}x + C\). (No modulus is needed on \(x^2 + 1\), which is always positive.)

rows.stem:
Find the shortest distance between the lines :
\(\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 9}{-3}\) and \(\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y + 15}{-7} = \dfrac{z - 9}{5}\).
rows.solution:
Read a point and a direction off each line and use the skew-lines formula \(\text{S.D.} = \dfrac{\left|(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}) \cdot (\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2})\right|}{\left|\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right|}\).
In vector form the lines are \(\vec{r} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 9\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k})\) and \(\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - 15\hat{j} + 9\hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 5\hat{k})\), so \(\vec{a_1} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 9\hat{k}\), \(\vec{b_1} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\), \(\vec{a_2} = 3\hat{i} - 15\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b_2} = 2\hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\). Then \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = 4\hat{i} - 16\hat{j}\), the \(\hat{k}\) components cancelling.
The cross product is \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = (5 - 21)\hat{i} - (10 + 6)\hat{j} + (-14 - 2)\hat{k} = -16\hat{i} - 16\hat{j} - 16\hat{k}\), whose magnitude is \(16\sqrt{3}\). Since it is non-zero the lines are not parallel.
The scalar triple product is \((\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}) \cdot (\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}) = 4(-16) + (-16)(-16) + 0(-16) = -64 + 256 = 192\).
Hence \(\text{S.D.} = \dfrac{|192|}{16\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{3}} = 4\sqrt{3}\) units. (The triple product is non-zero, confirming the lines are genuinely skew rather than intersecting.)

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the image A′ of the point A(2, 1, 2) in the line \(l : \vec{r} = 4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda\,(\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k})\). Also, find the equation of line joining AA′. Find the foot of perpendicular from point A on the line \(l\).
rows.solution:
Let P be the foot of the perpendicular from A on \(l\); it is also where \(AA'\) meets \(l\), and P is the mid-point of \(AA'\) because a point and its image are reflections in the line.
A general point of \(l\) is \((\lambda + 4,\ -\lambda + 2,\ -\lambda + 2)\). With \(A(2, 1, 2)\), the direction ratios of \(AP\) are \(\langle \lambda + 2,\ -\lambda + 1,\ -\lambda \rangle\).
Since \(AP \perp l\), the dot product of this with the direction \(\langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle\) of \(l\) is zero: \((\lambda + 2) - (-\lambda + 1) - (-\lambda) = 0\), i.e. \(3\lambda + 1 = 0\), so \(\lambda = -\dfrac{1}{3}\).
Substituting, the FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR is \(P\left(\dfrac{11}{3}, \dfrac{7}{3}, \dfrac{7}{3}\right)\).
Writing the image as \(A'(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) and using that P is the mid-point of \(AA'\): \(\dfrac{2 + \alpha}{2} = \dfrac{11}{3}\), \(\dfrac{1 + \beta}{2} = \dfrac{7}{3}\), \(\dfrac{2 + \gamma}{2} = \dfrac{7}{3}\), giving \(\alpha = \dfrac{16}{3}\), \(\beta = \dfrac{11}{3}\), \(\gamma = \dfrac{8}{3}\). So the IMAGE is \(A'\left(\dfrac{16}{3}, \dfrac{11}{3}, \dfrac{8}{3}\right)\).
For the LINE \(AA'\), its direction ratios are \(A' - A = \left\langle \dfrac{10}{3}, \dfrac{8}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3} \right\rangle\), so \(\dfrac{x - 2}{10/3} = \dfrac{y - 1}{8/3} = \dfrac{z - 2}{2/3}\). Scaling the direction ratios to \(\langle 5, 4, 1 \rangle\) gives the tidier form \(\dfrac{3(x - 2)}{5} = \dfrac{3(y - 1)}{4} = \dfrac{3(z - 2)}{1}\), equivalently \(\dfrac{x - 2}{5} = \dfrac{y - 1}{4} = \dfrac{z - 2}{1}\).
As a check, \(\langle 5, 4, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle = 5 - 4 - 1 = 0\), so \(AA'\) is indeed perpendicular to \(l\).

rows.stem:
Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 4 & 4 \\ -7 & 1 & 3 \\ 5 & -3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), find AB. Hence, solve the system of linear equations :
\(x - y + z = 4\)
\(x - 2y - 2z = 9\)
\(2x + y + 3z = 1\)
rows.solution:
First multiply the matrices. Working row by row, every off-diagonal entry cancels and every diagonal entry comes to 8, giving \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = 8I\). (For instance the first entry is \((-4)(1) + (4)(1) + (4)(2) = 8\) and the next in that row is \((-4)(-1) + (4)(-2) + (4)(1) = 0\).)
This is the whole point of the question: from \(AB = 8I\) it follows that \(B^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{8}A\), so \(B\) can be inverted without computing an adjoint.
Now observe that the coefficient matrix of the system is exactly \(B\), since the equations read \(x - y + z = 4\), \(x - 2y - 2z = 9\), \(2x + y + 3z = 1\). So the system is \(BX = C\) with \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and therefore \(X = B^{-1}C = \dfrac{1}{8}AC\).
Computing \(AC\): the rows give \((-4)(4) + (4)(9) + (4)(1) = 24\), \((-7)(4) + (1)(9) + (3)(1) = -16\), and \((5)(4) + (-3)(9) + (-1)(1) = -8\). Hence \(X = \dfrac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix} 24 \\ -16 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\).
So \(x = 3\), \(y = -2\), \(z = -1\). Substituting back: \(3 + 2 - 1 = 4\), \(3 + 4 + 2 = 9\) and \(6 - 2 - 3 = 1\), so all three equations are satisfied.

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem:
If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), then find \(A^{-1}\).
Hence, solve the system of linear equations :
\(x - 2y = 10\)
\(2x - y - z = 8\)
\(-2y + z = 7\)
rows.solution:
Expanding along the first row, \(|A| = 1\big[(-1)(1) - (-2)(-1)\big] - 2\big[(-2)(1) - (-2)(0)\big] + 0 = 1(-3) - 2(-2) = 1\). Since \(|A| = 1 \ne 0\), \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors are \(A_{11} = -3\), \(A_{12} = 2\), \(A_{13} = 2\), \(A_{21} = -2\), \(A_{22} = 1\), \(A_{23} = 1\), \(A_{31} = -4\), \(A_{32} = 2\), \(A_{33} = 3\). Transposing the cofactor matrix gives \(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), and since \(|A| = 1\), \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & -2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
Now look carefully at the system \(x - 2y = 10\), \(2x - y - z = 8\), \(-2y + z = 7\). Its coefficient matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), which is the TRANSPOSE of \(A\), not \(A\) itself. So the matrix equation is \(A^{T}X = B\) with \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 8 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(X = (A^{T})^{-1}B = (A^{-1})^{T}B\), using the fact that inverting and transposing commute.
Therefore \(X = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 8 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\). The rows give \(-30 + 16 + 14 = 0\), \(-20 + 8 + 7 = -5\) and \(-40 + 16 + 21 = -3\).
Hence \(x = 0\), \(y = -5\), \(z = -3\). Checking: \(0 + 10 = 10\), \(0 + 5 + 3 = 8\) and \(10 - 3 = 7\), so all three equations hold.

rows.solution: A relation from S to J is any SUBSET of the Cartesian product \(S \times J\), so the count is the number of subsets of that product. Here \(n(S) = 4\) and \(n(J) = 3\), so \(n(S \times J) = 4 \times 3 = 12\), and a set with 12 elements has \(2^{12}\) subsets. Hence the number of relations from S to J is \(2^{4 \times 3} = 2^{12} = 4096\).
